draft.title: Sentence structure and syntax
card: Short sentences
A short sentence can build tension or add emphasis. Example: "The door opened. Nobody was there." The pause after each full stop makes the reader hold their breath.
Long sentences

A long, layered sentence adds detail after detail. It can slow the reader down, or it can build momentum and pull them along. Example: "The tide crept up, swallowed the shells, and licked at the boat."
Fragments and lists
A fragment is a group of words that is not a full sentence. Example: "Silence. Again." It makes a thought land sharply. A list piles up items to suggest abundance or overload.
Inverted order
Inverted word order puts a word or phrase before its usual place. Example: "Gone was the summer." The unusual order draws attention to the idea placed first.
draft.remember: Writers shape how an idea lands by choosing how long, broken or ordered a sentence is.

a.q: A writer ends a scene with: "The phone rang. Once. Twice. Then nothing." What is the main effect of these very short sentences?
opts: They build tension through sharp pauses
They slow the pace with long descriptive detail
They suggest there are too many items to count
They reverse the usual order of words
a.why: Short sentences separated by full stops create pauses, so the reader waits for what comes next and feels tense. The sentences are not long or layered, so they do not slow the pace with detail.
a.clue: Think about what each full stop does to the reader's pace.

b.q: Read: "She packed the books, folded the coats, wrapped the plates, taped the boxes, and kept going." Which choice best describes the syntax and its effect?
opts: A long sentence that builds momentum through its actions
A short sentence that creates sudden emphasis
A fragment that makes a single thought land sharply
Inverted order that draws attention to the first word
b.why: The sentence is long and adds one action after another, so the reader is carried along as the work piles up. It is not short or a fragment, and the word order is the usual one, so it is not inverted.
b.clue: Count how many actions are joined in one sentence.

proposal.title: Sentence structure and syntax
card: Short sentences
A short sentence can build tension or add emphasis. Example: "The door opened. Nobody was there." The pause after each full stop makes the reader hold their breath.
Long sentences

A long, layered sentence adds detail after detail. It can slow the reader down, or it can build momentum and pull them along. Example: one sentence that follows a tide creeping up, swallowing shells and reaching a boat, with no full stop until the end.
Fragments and lists
A fragment is a group of words that is not a full sentence. Example: "Silence. Again." It makes a thought land sharply. A list piles up items to suggest abundance or overload.
Inverted order
Inverted word order puts a word or phrase before its usual place. Example: "Gone was the summer." The unusual order draws attention to the idea placed first.
proposal.remember: Writers shape how an idea lands by choosing how long, broken or ordered a sentence is.

a.q: A writer ends a scene with: "The phone rang. Once. Twice. Then nothing." What is the main effect of these short sentences and fragments?
opts: They build tension through sharp pauses
They slow the pace with long descriptive detail
They suggest there are too many items to count
They reverse the usual order of words
a.why: A short sentence followed by fragments creates a pause at each full stop, so the reader waits for what comes next and feels tense. Nothing here is long or layered, so the pace is not slowed by detail.
a.clue: Think about what each full stop does to the reader's pace.

b.q: A writer describes Ava moving house in one long sentence. It joins task after task with commas and has no full stop until the end. What is the main effect?
opts: It builds momentum as the tasks pile up
It creates a sharp pause before each new task
It makes a single thought land sharply
It draws attention to the word placed first
b.why: A long sentence that adds one task after another, without stopping, carries the reader along as the work piles up. Sharp pauses come from full stops and short sentences, which this sentence avoids until the end.
b.clue: Does the reader get a chance to stop before the end?
